presentingComplaint: Sudden, explosive, worst-ever headache peaking within seconds, with brief loss of consciousness and vomiting.
history: Previously well 52-year-old woman developed an abrupt, severe occipital headache while straining at stool that reached maximal intensity almost instantly ('thunderclap'). She had transient loss of consciousness for under a minute, followed by two episodes of vomiting, photophobia and neck pain. No preceding trauma. Reports a milder self-limiting 'sentinel' headache 10 days earlier that she did not seek care for. Risk factors: long-standing hypertension (poorly controlled), current smoker (20 pack-years), and a mother with a 'brain bleed'. No anticoagulant use.
examination: Alert but distressed, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), photophobic. Neck stiffness with positive Kernig sign; no focal limb deficit; pupils equal and reactive; no papilloedema acutely; fundoscopy shows a small subhyaloid haemorrhage. No fever, no rash. Pertinent negatives: no facial/limb weakness, no dysarthria, no signs of meningeal infection, cardiovascular and respiratory exams unremarkable.

labs.ecg: sinus rhythm with deep symmetric T-wave inversions and prolonged QT

imaging: Non-contrast CT head: hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures and interhemispheric fissure — diffuse aneurysmal-pattern subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT angiography demonstrates a 7 mm saccular aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery.
finalDiagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (anterior communicating artery aneurysm)
citations: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage 2023
contraindications: Avoid antiplatelet/anticoagulant agents before aneurysm is secured
Nimodipine may cause hypotension — titrate carefully; caution in renal/hepatic impairment
Aggressive BP lowering below recommended targets risks cerebral ischaemia
edgeCases: Non-contrast CT sensitivity falls after 6 hours; a normal CT beyond this window requires lumbar puncture for xanthochromia (spectrophotometry) to exclude SAH
Sentinel ('warning') headache days earlier is easily dismissed
Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH has a benign course and negative angiography
expectedMaiK: A thunderclap, worst-ever headache with meningism and transient loss of consciousness is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise; obtain an urgent non-contrast CT head immediately and, if negative beyond 6 hours, perform lumbar puncture for xanthochromia. Do not give antiplatelets/anticoagulation before the aneurysm is secured.
expectedNextQuestions: Was the headache truly instantaneous ('like a thunderclap') and the worst of your life?
Any preceding sentinel headache, neck pain, or transient loss of consciousness?
Any family history of aneurysm/SAH, polycystic kidney disease, or anticoagulant use?
expectedInvestigations: Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT negative and >6h from onset

investigations: Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT negative
